### acm-certificates-regional

**Claim.** ACM certificates are Regional resources: to use the same domain names with Elastic Load Balancing in more than one Region, you request or import a certificate in each Region, and you cannot copy a certificate between Regions.

**Write it as.** `Certificates in ACM are regional resources` · `You cannot copy a certificate between regions`

**Scope.** per Region.

> "Certificates in ACM are regional resources. To use a certificate with Elastic Load Balancing for the same fully qualified domain name (FQDN) or set of FQDNs in more than one AWS region, you must request or import a certificate for each region. For certificates provided by ACM, this means you must revalidate each domain name in the certificate for each region. You cannot copy a certificate between regions."
> — [What is AWS Certificate Manager?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-overview.html)

**Claim.** A renewal status of Failed means one or more domain names were not validated before the certificate expired and ACM did not renew it; Pending validation means you must act to validate the domain names or the certificate will not be renewed.

**Write it as.** `ACM did not renew the certificate` · `You must take action to validate`

**Scope.** per certificate.

> "One or more domain names were not validated before the certificate expired, and ACM did not renew the certificate."
> — [Check a certificate's renewal status](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/check-certificate-renewal-status.html)

> "ACM couldn't automatically validate one or more domain names in the certificate. You must take action to validate these domain names or the certificate won't be renewed."
> — [Check a certificate's renewal status](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/check-certificate-renewal-status.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### acm-three-certificate-types

**Claim.** ACM supports three types of certificates: public certificates trusted across the internet, private certificates that are not publicly trusted and are used inside an organization, and imported certificates from third-party certificate authorities.

**Write it as.** `supports three types of certificates` · `Publicly trusted across the internet`

**Scope.** per certificate.

> "AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports three types of certificates."
> — [Types of certificates in AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/certificate-types.html)

> "Publicly trusted across the internet. Public certificates issued by ACM are trusted by all major browsers and operating systems, making them suitable for securing public-facing websites and applications."
> — [Types of certificates in AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/certificate-types.html)

> "Not publicly trusted. Private certificates are primarily used internal to an organization, such as for encrypting internal traffic, authenticating services, or implementing mutual TLS (mTLS) between microservices."
> — [Types of certificates in AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/certificate-types.html)

> "Customer-owned certificates imported into ACM. You can import certificates obtained from third-party certificate authorities for use with ACM integrated services or for export."
> — [Types of certificates in AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/certificate-types.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### acm-wildcard-one-level-not-apex

**Claim.** In a wildcard certificate the asterisk must be leftmost and protects only one subdomain level, and *.example.com protects only subdomains, not the apex example.com; request both names to cover both.

**Write it as.** `protects only one subdomain level` · `not the bare or apex domain`

**Scope.** per wildcard certificate.

> "In a wildcard certificate, the asterisk (`*`) must be leftmost in the domain name and protects only one subdomain level. For instance, `*.example.com` protects `login.example.com` and `test.example.com`, but not `test.login.example.com`. Also, `*.example.com` protects *only* subdomains, not the bare or apex domain (`example.com`). You can request a certificate for both a bare domain and its subdomains by specifying multiple domain names, such as `example.com` and `*.example.com`."
> — [AWS Certificate Manager public certificate characteristics and limitations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-certificate-characteristics.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

**Scope.** per certificate.

> "ACM certificates can secure singular domain names, multiple specific domain names, wildcard domains, or combinations of these. ACM wildcard certificates can protect an unlimited number of subdomains."
> — [What is AWS Certificate Manager?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-overview.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.
